equivalents.note: The Tibetan has the moon 'joined to the string' (zla ba rgyud la sbyar); rgyud is also the ordinary word for tantra, so it is too common to search on.
The Tibetan line has dbyig drang, 'straight staff', where the Bengali has dāṇḍī bāki; drang stands where bāki (perhaps 'bent') stands, a difference worth checking.
The Tibetan line addresses a plain 'friend' (kye'i grogs), while its comment has the feminine grogs mo and names her bdag med ma (cp.17.m2).
The Tibetan reads ruṇā as if it were karuṇā, 'compassion' (snying rje sgrogs pa can, 'proclaiming compassion'); snying rje is the regular equivalent of karuṇā, so it cannot be claimed for this term.
The Tibetan line reads karahā and karahaka as 'wood and little wood' (shing dang shing bu), apparently parts of the vīṇā; shing (wood, tree, and a clause connective) is too common to search on.
The Tibetan line has no word for batiśa, 'thirty-two', before the strings, though its comment has rtsa sum cu so gnyis (cp.17.m4).
The Tibetan reads the Buddha drama as 'the Buddha's dance' (sangs rgyas gar), the same word gar that renders nṛtya in the comment, and has 'especially difficult' (khyad par nyid du dka') for bisamā.

The Tibetan comment renders vajrapadanṛtya as 'the dance of the vajra steps' (rdo rje'i rkang stabs kyi gar) and nṛtyate in the Dvikalpa quote as gar nyid; gar also renders nāṭaka in 5b, so it cannot be claimed for one term alone.
The Tibetan renders caryāntaram, 'another caryā', as glu dbyangs gzhan, 'another song', using the word it uses for rāga in the song headings.
Only the first of Munidatta's two 'tathā cāgamaḥ' has a Tibetan counterpart (lung las kyang); the Tibetan runs the two quoted verses together.
The Tibetan has 'the essential letter a' (snying po'i yi ge a) for sārākṣaram akāraṃ and a ni in the Nāmasaṃgīti quote; the bare syllable also sits inside a wa d+hU tI, so it is not searchable.
The Tibetan has mi 'gyur ba'i ngo bo nyid, 'unchanging nature', for akṣarasvarūpa, reading akṣara as 'unchanging'.
For bhāvasvarūpa the Tibetan has ngo bo nyid kyi rang bzhin, so here svarūpa seems to be rang bzhin and bhāva ngo bo nyid, the reverse of the pairing in cp.17.m3.

The Tibetan comment cites the passage as kA li zhes bya ba where the Sanskrit has javem ityādi, calls karaha 'nose-wood' (sna'i shing), and has 'the camel of the mind' (sems kyi rnga mong), as if reading cittoṣṭra for cittauṣṇya.
rtsa sum cu so gnyis renders dvātriṃśannāḍī, 'thirty-two channels'; rtsa (also 'root', 'grass') is too common to search on.

questions: sunyata (suna) in cp.17.2b: the Tibetan line (rgyud kyi sgra nyid snying rje sgrogs pa can) has no word for 'empty'; sgra nyid, 'the sound itself', stands where the Bengali has suna tānti dhani, so either the translator did not read suna or nyid is all that is left of it. Not matched in the line; the comment's stong pa nyid (cp.17.m2) is already matched.

nrtya (nācanti) in cp.17.5a: the Tibetan line (rgyal po gang byed lha mo glu len byed) has no word for dancing. gang byed, 'does whatever', may be a slip for gar byed, 'dances', and rgyal po, 'king', stands where the Bengali has bājila, perhaps read as rāja-; so the dance was matched in the comment (cp.17.m5) instead.

p-rahu (prabhāsvararāhukeṇa) in cp.17.m4: the Tibetan has no sgra gcan; it has 'od gsal 'dren pas, 'as it draws clear light', which looks like a reading vāhaka, 'carrier', for rāhuka (r and v differ by only a dot in Bengali script). Not matched.
